summary: Deep-dive workshop to align on a reproducible benchmark methodology. transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-07 14:30 PST - Duration ~63 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Morales (Aurelia Head of ML), Samir Chopra (Platform Eng), Olivia Chen (CTO)
Files referenced: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness (private), https://redwood.app/benchmarks/aurelia-methods-v1.xlsx, slide deck: /shared/benchmark-methods-deck.pdf

00:00 Marcus (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick agenda — Priya will walk through the harness and recommended protocols, then we'll go into prompt set design, load gen, and finish with VPC/on-prem considerations and open Q&A.
00:18 Olivia (Aurelia): Great, thanks. We're mostly focused on latency tail and ensuring our KV cache behavior doesn't introduce flakiness, and want an apples-to-apples path between hosted and on-prem runs.
00:30 Priya (Redwood SE): Awesome. I'll start with the harness. We provide a load harness that supports session-level replay, so you can preserve context length and inter-message timing. Common pitfall: folks replay token-level traffic but they don't reproduce the session warmup pattern — so KV-cash — sorry, KV cache — is cold and results look worse.
00:52 Dr. Elena: Yeah we've seen that. In our internal tests, first 20 requests are super slow, then it settles. We worry about realistic warmup being costly in cloud runs.
01:05 Priya: Right — recommended approach: define a warmup window per virtual user. For example, for a 4-turn chat session, run an N-warmup of 2 full sessions, discard metrics for those. Then measure steady-state p50/p95/p99 across the next M sessions. We usually define buckets by sequence-length: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-512), long (>512). That helps avoid p99 skew if 10% of traffic is very long.
01:40 Samir: How do you handle tokenizer differences? We have internal tokenizers with custom tokens; mismatch causes token count variance.
01:50 Priya: Good question. Two options: 1) canonicalize to a single tokenizer when comparing. We'll use the same tokenizer binary across runs — Redwood can mount your tokenizer or we can export tokenized byte offsets. 2) Or measure both 'raw chars' and 'tokenized tokens' columns in the spreadsheet to normalize throughput per-token. The apples-to-apples rule is: same tokenizer, same prompt pre-processing.
02:18 Marcus: Also record model config: sequence length truncation policy, special-token handling, and any system/preamble tokens. Differences here will blow the comparison.
02:30 Dr. Elena: About KV cache: do you measure hit rate as a function of session similarity? Our sessions are patient-specific and reuse histories sometimes, so it'll vary.
02:44 Priya: We capture a KV-cache-hit metric per request — it's basically whether the runtime served from the prefix cache (exact-match) or had to regenerate. For reproducible results, you should create a synthetic shared prefix fraction: e.g., 30% shared prefix across requests to simulate templated prompts, 70% unique. We'll run experiments sweeping shared-prefix %. That surfaces the marginal benefit of KV caching.
03:10 Olivia: Okay. On quantization: we care about FP16 vs 8-bit quantized. Does Redwood provide automatic QA for hallucination risk?
03:22 Priya: We have quality hooks. For apples-to-apples you must fix the same random seeds and sampling params. In quantization runs, we'll include a small eval subset (10-20 prompts) to check log-prob differences and a quality score (BLEU/ROUGE-ish or human-in-the-loop). Note q8.1 vs q8.2 can have discrete token shifts, so compute top-k overlap and a semantic similarity metric (embedding cosine) for robustness.
03:55 Samir: For load generation, what's your typical ramp profile? We don't want cold-start spikes.
04:05 Priya: We recommend three phases: 1) ramp (5-15 minutes) exponential to target QPS, 2) steady-state (30-60 minutes) at target QPS, 3) burst tests with short windows (1-2 minutes) at 2-3x QPS. Keep overall run under the account limits. Also important: align concurrency and request-size distribution (we'll provide a per-minute inter-arrival distribution file).
04:40 Marcus: Note on batching: Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching; we can control max batch size and batch timeout. For apples-to-apples, you should assert identical batching policy across runs (max_batch_tokens or max_batch_items and timeout_ms). If you change hardware, batching dynamics change; capture average batch size and waiting time.
05:05 Dr. Elena: Can you show what metrics we'll get back from the harness?
05:12 Priya: Sure — the harness emits: request_id, timestamp, input_tokens, output_tokens, model_variant, seq_len, batch_size_at_send, batch_wait_ms, kv_cache_hit, gpu_util, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, tokens_per_sec, and quality_score. We'll also export raw logs for debugging.
05:40 Olivia: How accurate are p99 numbers for short runs? We need reliability to make procurement decisions.
05:48 Priya: Short runs are noisy. p99 needs lots of samples — we recommend at least 10k requests for stable p99. If your product traffic is lower, consider synthetic amplification (replaying user sessions with jitter) but ensure you don't artificially inflate cache hit rates.
06:10 Samir: For VPC/on-prem runs, what telemetry can you collect? We're sensitive about data egress.
06:18 Marcus: We can do two modes: 1) agent-light: Redwood sends a small telemetry bundle (metrics only, no payload). 2) Full-run artifacts on a shared S3 in your account (you control access). For on-prem we can run the harness locally and you can upload sanitized metrics. We'll sign an NDA addendum if needed.
06:40 Dr. Elena: Token-level privacy is key; can we mask prompt content before sending?
06:45 Priya: Yes — the harness supports client-side hashing of inputs and also sending only token lengths and embedding hashes. For quality checks we need some raw samples; we can do human-reviewed redaction.
06:58 Olivia: Any gotchas for apples-to-apples with different hardware (A100 vs H100 vs V100)?
07:06 Priya: Yes — kernel differences and attention kernels change latency profiles. Key guidelines: use identical batch-timeout semantics, same model variant (e.g., same quantization libs), and measure per-token throughput normalized to effective FLOPs. Also capture GPU topology and driver versions as metadata. We'll put those in the benchmark sheet.
07:35 Marcus: We'll also log kernel names; sometimes ops get fused on newer drivers, which is fine, but you need to know that change happened.
07:44 Samir: On batch shaping: if we use session-level batching vs per-request batching, what changes most?
07:52 Priya: Session-level preserves context and leads to higher KV-cache hit rates and larger average batch sizes, improving tokens/sec but potentially increasing latency tail if a single long session joins a batch. So we recommend tracking batch size distribution and isolating long sessions into separate buckets during analysis.
08:18 Dr. Elena: Let's talk quantitatively — what's a realistic acceptance criteria for our pilot? We aim for p95 <= 350ms on medium sequences and p99 <= 750ms; throughput target of 1200 tokens/sec aggregated. Are those reasonable?
08:35 Priya: They might be achievable on Dedicated H100 with q8.2 for many models. We should define "medium" precisely (e.g., 128-256 tokens). We'll run a baseline hosted and then a VPC run to compare. If p99 fails on VPC, check network variance and batch-timeout settings.
09:00 Olivia: For apples-to-apples we also want consistent scoring for hallucinations. How do we instrument that automatically?
09:08 Priya: Use an embedding-similarity based sentinel: compute embedding of reference response and candidate, and threshold by cosine. Also track token-level log-prob shifts between variants. We will include a human-review sample of 50 responses per run.
09:28 Marcus: Practical note — when you send the prompt set, include annotations: intent, expected output length, and any safety constraints. That helps us create metric filters.
09:40 Dr. Elena: We'll send an initial 150 prompts with tags: triage, billing, notes-summarization. Some have domain tokens (med IDs) that might be rare.
09:52 Priya: Rare tokens amplify quantization differences — we'll flag those.
10:00 Samir: About reproducibility: do you pin seeds and samplers? We use nucleus sampling for prod.
10:08 Priya: Yes — for comparison fix the sampling method — e.g., greedy or top-k with seed. For production variance-run tests keep sampling on but compare statistical distributions across runs. For deterministic evals use greedy to compare tokenization and logits.
10:26 Olivia: Network jitter in VPCs is a concern; how do you separate that from runtime scheduling?
10:34 Priya: We collect in-host and end-to-end latencies. In the harness we'll emit latency broken down: client->edge, edge->inference-start, inference-end->response. If network jitter dominates, you'll see variance in the first bucket. We'll also run a pure local loopback test to baseline the runtime.
10:56 Dr. Elena: Any advice on how to design the 'apples-to-apples' naming convention for variants to avoid confusion?
11:02 Marcus: We use a variant tag schema: modelName_quantBackend_quantOpts_hardware_batchPolicy_date. Example: llama2-13b_q8.2_noFp16_H100_mbs256to128_20251107. Keep that across runs.
11:18 Priya: We'll also checksum the model artifact and tokenizer and include those in results.
11:24 Samir: Can Redwood run a short sanity run today?
11:28 Marcus: We can run a small 1k request run with synthetic prompts if you give us access. Preferably in the dev VPC. That gives us a baseline within 24 hours.
11:38 Olivia: We'll need to loop legal in on the VPC peering — provisioning can take a few days.
11:44 Dr. Elena: We also want to examine KV cache eviction policy. How do you surface evictions?
11:50 Priya: We log cache insert and eviction events with timestamps and key sizes. For LRU policies you'll see evictions when memory pressure rises. We'll plot hit-rate vs working set size. For deterministic experiments, freeze eviction thresholds.
12:08 Marcus: Quick callouts on measurement noise: disable background tasks on the test nodes, pin CPU governors, and isolate the GPUs. We'll provide an infra checklist.
12:20 Samir: Great. What about cost accounting per run so we can justify Dedicated?
12:26 Priya: The harness outputs tokens-per-dollar estimates by combining our runtime token/time with instance pricing. We'll produce a cost delta table between hosted shared and dedicated reserved capacity.
12:40 Olivia: Anything else we should watch for?
12:43 Marcus: Look out for cold-starts in model-forking scenarios — if you spin up multiple variants concurrently, the first requests pay the load overhead. Staggered start helps.
12:54 Dr. Elena: Thanks — this is helpful. We'll compile the prompt set and schedule the VPC window.
13:00 Marcus: Recap of next steps: Marcus upload harness + readme, Priya schedule VPC test, Dr. Elena provide prompts, Samir provision peering. We'll reconvene after the initial run to interpret results.
13:16 Olivia: Thanks all.
13:20 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional words mis-heard (KV cash -> KV cache), speaker overlap at 07:40 with small crosstalk, punctuation inconsistent.
